title: A green check isn't enough
dek: Xeno puts an AI agent's verification state on its Herdr row, and on the claim's line in your editor.

evidence.note: The plugin's tests start a Herdr server and read each pane's lights back. They run in CI but don't gate it yet.
The agents' diffs and Jev's scores are recordings, replayed through the real plugin.

evidence.what: A live run, agents and Jev included
evidence.note: When it runs, it goes on this site as a check, with its prediction registered first.

blocks: An agent tells me people can install witness, my language server for verification findings. The check is green.
Here is what the check ran:

blocks.text:
$ cd /tmp/feature && bash install.sh
Installing Go 1.24 for witness...
witness installed to /usr/local/bin/witness

blocks: Nobody installs witness that way. People add the dev container feature, and the feature gets Go from another feature it depends on. The check ran the install script in a container that already had what it needed, so it would have passed whether or not that dependency worked.
The check wasn't wrong about what it saw. It just couldn't have failed.

sections.heading: A check is one arm
blocks: A passing check is a verifier: it goes looking for the claim being true. On its own it can't tell you whether it was able to see the claim being false.

For that you need a falsifier: a run that tries to make the claim false. Here, that means removing the dependency and installing the feature again. If the install still succeeds, the check never had teeth. If it breaks, the check can fail, and its pass starts to mean something.

Two arms still aren't enough when an agent runs both. An agent can report a falsifier that didn't really try. So a third reader, Jev, gets both arms' diffs and is asked how likely it is that both were genuine.

sections.heading: Three lights
blocks: Xeno is a plugin for Herdr, a terminal multiplexer for agents. An agent reports each arm from inside its own pane:

blocks.text:
xeno verifier confirmed   # or failed
xeno falsifier failed     # or refuted
xeno jev 0.9              # Jev: were both arms genuine?

blocks: Each agent's row in the Herdr sidebar gets three lights, in the order of a window's: red for the falsifier, amber for Jev, green for the verifier. A lit light means that arm ran. Red isn't bad news and green isn't good news.
Next to the lights is a status. Only two of them call for attention:

blocks.text:
uncontrolled  an arm hasn't reported
unverified    both reported; Jev missing or below 0.7
confirmed     on target; verifier confirmed, falsifier failed
refuted       on target; the falsifier won
inconclusive  on target; neither arm got its way

blocks: A refuted run is on target. The prediction lost, but it was tested, and that's the point.

sections.heading: The witness check, three times
blocks: Name where the claim lives and xeno also writes a witness finding on that line, so the verdict shows up in the editor, with each arm's diff a go-to-definition away.

blocks.text:
$ xeno claim check.go:9
$ xeno verifier confirmed today.diff
uncontrolled

blocks: First, today's green check on its own. One arm has reported, so the run is uncontrolled: a warning on the claim's line.

blocks.text:
$ xeno falsifier failed falsifier.diff
$ xeno jev 0.3
unverified

blocks: Then the falsifier removes the dependency, and the install breaks. Both arms have reported now, but Jev reads them side by side and doubts that the verifier installed witness the way people do. The run is unverified, and the warning becomes an error.

blocks.text:
$ xeno verifier confirmed verifier.diff
$ xeno jev 0.9
confirmed

blocks: Last, a verifier that installs it properly: it brings a dev container up with the witness feature and finds the binary. Jev is satisfied, the run is confirmed, and the finding drops to information.
The check was green all three times. Xeno said three different things.

sections.heading: What this is and isn't
blocks: The example above is a replay. The diffs are recordings of agent runs, and Jev's scores are recordings too. What's real is the plugin: it runs in Herdr, lights the panes and writes the findings, and its tests check that against a running Herdr server.

So this article shows how xeno reads a run, not that a live agent and a live Jev get this one right. That's the next check, and it will be on this site with its prediction written down before it runs, whichever way it goes.
The source is in null-hype/features, under src/xeno.
